summary: Describes how to use Transport Layer Security to protect Common Open Policy Service (COPS) connections. It also updates RFC 2748 by changing the contents of the Client-Accept message. It is a standards-track memo.

eli5.summary: COPS carries policy messages between network devices. This memo wraps those messages in a locked envelope so nobody can read or change them in transit.

questions: how to secure cops with tls
how does cops start a tls handshake
what is the integrity tls object in cops
subtitle: How a policy server and its devices upgrade a plain COPS connection to a TLS-protected one.

tldr.problem: COPS distributes policy from a central server to network devices, but its own security only protects per-hop integrity. Sensitive policy also needs confidentiality, because policy can cross domain boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The two sides connect on the standard COPS port, then use a new Integrity-TLS object in Client-Open or Client-Accept messages to signal that a TLS handshake should start. After the handshake, all COPS data travels as TLS application data.
tldr.outcome: COPS/TLS behaves like COPS over TCP apart from connection setup, with X.509 certificates identifying the endpoints. The RFC updates RFC 2748 and has itself been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4261 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2748 and has itself been updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why COPS Needs TLS
sections.content:
COPS (Common Open Policy Service, RFC 2748) was designed to distribute clear-text policy information from a central Policy Decision Point (PDP) to a set of Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs). It has its own security mechanisms, but they protect the per-hop integrity of the policy only.

Some uses, such as distributing security policy, also need data confidentiality. Organizations may want to hide some or all of their policies, especially when policy reaches devices such as mobile platforms that can cross domain boundaries. This RFC adds TLS, which offers one- and two-way authentication, dynamic session keying, and data stream privacy and integrity.

The idea is deliberately simple: use COPS over TLS the way you would use COPS over TCP. Apart from a specific procedure to initialize the connection, there is no difference between COPS/TLS and COPS/TCP.
sections.eli5: COPS is a boss telling devices what rules to follow. Without protection, anyone along the way could peek at the rules. TLS puts the messages in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Separate Ports or Upward Negotiation
sections.content:
There are two ways to run secure and insecure versions of a protocol side by side. With separate ports, the secure version gets its own well-known port. This needs no changes to existing insecure implementations, but it does not scale well because every secure protocol needs another port. RFC 2595 lists more problems with it.

With upward negotiation, both versions share one port. The client connects, the two sides discover each other's capabilities, and security negotiation starts if desired. This usually means changing the protocol being secured.

Because of the many issues with separate ports, the authors chose upward negotiation for COPS/TLS. The PEP therefore connects to the standard COPS port first, and security is negotiated inside COPS messages.
sections.eli5: Instead of building a second front door just for secure visitors, everyone comes through the same door and then agrees whether to go into the private room.

sections.title: The Integrity-TLS Object and Error Codes
sections.content:
The TLS Message Integrity object (Integrity-TLS) is how either side starts TLS negotiation. It has C-Num 16 and C-Type 2. It should be included only in Client-Open or Client-Accept messages and MUST NOT appear in any other COPS message. The object carries a 16-bit Flags field, and the only flag defined is 0x01 (StartTLS), meaning the sender wishes to start a TLS handshake. The reserved field is set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

Any message containing this object MUST use Client-Type 0. That client type is used for connection-level security and only during connection establishment.

Two error codes from RFC 2748 are used. Error code 13 (Unknown COPS Object) signals a security-related closure when a side cannot support TLS; the sub-code then names C-Num 16 and C-Type 2. Error code 15 (Authentication Required) is sent when the PDP wants a different security mechanism than the PEP asked for. Its sub-code gives C-Num 16 and the preferred C-Type, or C-Type zero if the server supports no form of COPS security.
sections.eli5: The object is a little flag on the first messages that says "let's put on the secure envelope now". If someone cannot do that, they send back a note saying why.

sections.title: Starting a Secure Connection
sections.content:
Either side may start the negotiation. A PEP uses Client-Open (Client-Type 0, with Integrity-TLS), and the PDP SHOULD answer with a Client-Accept that also carries Integrity-TLS. A PDP can start it by putting Integrity-TLS in its Client-Accept after a plain Client-Open. Once the PEP receives the Client-Accept with the object, it SHOULD start the TLS handshake. Afterwards all COPS data MUST be sent as TLS application data.

This is why the RFC updates RFC 2748: the Client-Accept message may now carry an Integrity object with C-Type 2. The RFC says this new form does not replace or obsolete the existing Client-Accept, which can still be used for non-secure sessions.

If the PDP does not want a secure connection, it MUST reply with Client-Close using error code 15 and close the connection. A PEP that requires the object and does not see it in the Client-Accept MUST close the connection. In the PDP-initiated case, the PEP MUST NOT send any messages until the handshake completes, and the PDP MUST answer any that arrive early with Client-Close and error code 15.

A PDP that wants security on an existing non-secure connection sends Client-Close with error code 15 (C-Num 16, C-Type 2) and waits for the PEP to reconnect.
sections.eli5: One side says "want to switch to the secret code?" and the other says yes. Only then do they shake hands on the code, and nothing else is said before that.

sections.title: Closing a TLS Connection
sections.content:
TLS can close a connection securely: receiving a valid closure alert assures an implementation that no more data will arrive. A connection closed after sending only your own closure alert is an incomplete close, and COPS/TLS makes no use of TLS session reuse in that case. A connection closed without any closure alert is a premature close. It does not call into question data already received, but later data may have been cut off. Because TLS does not know COPS message boundaries, the COPS message header must be examined to tell whether truncation happened.

PEPs MUST treat premature closes as errors and received data as potentially truncated, and SHOULD recover gracefully from an incomplete close. PEPs SHOULD send a closure alert first. PDPs SHOULD expect incomplete closes, since a PEP often shuts down for reasons unrelated to policy transfer. PDPs MUST try to exchange closure alerts before closing.
sections.eli5: Saying goodbye properly lets the other side know the conversation really ended. Hanging up without a word might mean part of the message was lost.

sections.title: Identity, Access Control and Cipher Suite
sections.content:
Every PEP implementation MUST support an access control mechanism to identify authorized PDPs, and deployments SHOULD require it. PDP implementations MUST also support access control for PEPs, but deployments may choose not to use it when the policy is not sensitive. Endpoints MUST be identified with X.509 v3 certificates conforming to RFC 3280, and certificate verification MUST follow that RFC.

The PDP identity comes from the certificate's subjectAltName extension: a dNSName or iPAddress if present (with dNSName preferred when both are), otherwise the most specific Common Name. When PEPs are not access controlled, only the PDP is authenticated (one-way). When they are, both sides authenticate (two-way) and the PDP applies the same identity checks to the PEP.

PEPs MUST be able to securely acquire the trust anchor for each Certification Authority that issues PDP certificates, plus a list of authorized PDPs. If the PDP name does not match the certificate, an unattended PEP MUST log the error and terminate the connection with a bad certificate error.

For ciphers, implementations MUST support TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA. All other cipher suites are optional.
sections.eli5: Both sides can show an ID card to prove who they are. The device must always check that the boss's ID is real, so it does not take orders from a stranger.

sections.title: Security Notes, IANA and Compatibility
sections.content:
Both PDP and PEP MUST check the results of the TLS negotiation to see whether authentication and privacy are acceptable. If algorithms or key lengths are unacceptable, either side MAY terminate the connection.

The RFC warns of a man-in-the-middle attack that deletes the Integrity-TLS object or alters the Client-Open or Client-Accept messages. If security is required, the bootstrap policy of both sides must say so, and implementations should reject Client-Open or Client-Accept messages that lack the object.

PEPs and PDPs SHOULD stay backward compatible with peers that do not support COPS/TLS, and SHOULD handle the errors those peers return. IANA registered C-Num 16 / C-Type 2 (Integrity-TLS), the StartTLS flag value 0x01 for Client-Type 0, and the sub-codes for error code 15 (16/0 for no security, 16/2 for Integrity-TLS).
sections.eli5: A sneaky person might try to remove the "let's be secure" note. So devices that need security must insist on seeing it, and refuse to talk if it is missing.

fields.name: Length (Octets)
fields.desc: Length of the object in octets.

fields.name: C-Num
fields.desc: Object number for the Integrity object.

fields.name: C-Type
fields.desc: Selects the TLS version of the Integrity object.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: 0x01 = StartTLS: the sender wishes to start a TLS handshake.

messages.label: TLS handshake
messages.note: Further messages follow once the handshake completes.
